ETV_notes: 10 new eclipse times presented. Best model includes two circumbinary Jovian planets plus a quadratic trend with a longer period. Planetary periods favour a 2:1 ratio. Both planetary eccentricities are non-zero. Dynamical stability analysis leaves only 1 in 79700 models stable for more than 1 Myr. The quadratic term is in the direction of a lengthening orbital period and cannot be explained by magnetic braking or gravitational wave emission; it could be attributed to a third, more distant, circumbinary object. Some form of Applegate's mechanism could also be at work. Secondary eclipse O-C variations follow the proposed model, ruling out apsidal precession. The best test of the planetary model will come in 2018-2019.
PrimarySecondaryETVRelation: Secondary eclipse O-C variations follow the same proposed model as primary
ETV_reference: ["Brinkworth et al. 2006", "Qian et al. 2009", "Beuermann et al. 2010", "Beuermann et al. 2013a", "Marsh et al. 2014", "Parsons et al. 2014"]

Name: QS Vir
ETV_selection_reason: Shows eclipse time variations with large amplitudes and occasional extreme changes
ETV_notes: 86 published mid-eclipse times and 24 unpublished timings. O-C variations are large and erratic; a local or absolute maximum may have been reached. Previous explanations: Qian et al. (2010) proposed a combination of a large continuous decrease in orbital period and a circumbinary planet of ~7 MJup, but new data quickly showed this hypothesis wrong. Almeida & Jablonski (2011) presented a new fit. Applegate's mechanism was shown to be insufficient by Qian et al. following Brinkworth et al. Observations in coming years will determine whether O-C variations are cyclic.
ETV_reference: ["Qian et al. 2010", "Parsons et al. 2010b", "Almeida & Jablonski 2011", "Brinkworth et al. 2006"]

Third body confirmed by Lu (1992): P=49.50±0.36 yr, A=0.0082 d, projected distance of eclipsing pair from triple-system center of mass 1.78±0.16 AU, mass function 0.0023(7), M=0.21(2) Msol assuming coplanar orbit, a=15.75(7) AU, maximum angular separation 0.091(28) arcsec, Mbol=10.23(27), M3 red dwarf. Fourth body from Yang et al. (2014): P=27.40(24) yr, A=0.0051(2) d, f(m4)=0.0009(1), M4=0.151(75) Msol, angular separation 0.0615(183) arcsec, Mbol=11.22(14), likely M4 red dwarf. Residuals after two sinusoidal fits show another modulation with roughly P=19.5 yr and A=0.004 d, but cannot be attributed to another object. Name: Algol
ETV_selection_reason: O-C analysis detects multiple periodic signals interpreted as LTTE from companion candidates
ETV_notes: DCM detected six periodic signals in the O-C data, interpreted as LTTE from wide orbit companion candidates (Table 1): p1=680.4±0.4 d, A1=0.0064±0.0007 d (Algol C); p2=7290±29 d, A2=0.007±0.001 d (Algol D); p3=10145±30 d, A3=0.0097±0.0004 d (Algol E); p4=12294±109 d, A4=0.018±0.001 d (Algol F); p5=24246±872 d, A5=0.018±0.002 d (Algol G); p6=79999±1216 d, A6=0.287±0.005 d (Algol H). Mass and semi-major axis estimates for i=90,60,30 are given in Table 1. The p1 signal is 44.8 times weaker than p6, and differs 1.4 sigma from the known orbital period of Algol C. The paper emphasizes that m3 and a3 estimates rest on four assumptions: LTTE origin, Configuration 1, circular orbits, and treating each candidate as a single third body. No regular long-term period increase has been observed; Algol's orbital period has been constant for 236 years, Porb=2.86732870 d, producing a linear O-C change of 0.256 d. The lower limit for Algol C mass is 1.2 Msun at i=90, smaller than interferometric estimates.

ETV_notes: 40 new times of minima from 2017 Oct to 2019 Sep. Previous predictions include LTT period 7.15 yr and amplitude 92.4 s (Qian et al. 2009), revised period 8.87 yr and companion mass 32 MJ (Qian et al.), and Bogensberger et al. (2017) period 11.8 yr and e=0.38. New data are inconsistent with earlier circumbinary predictions and show a quadratic trend. Reduced chi2 quadratic fit is 1.62 vs linear 2.75, but Mann-Whitney U test shows no strong preference at p(0.05). Eq.1 quadratic ephemeris uses Q=5.5(9)e-13 day; recent quadratic coefficient is 3.98e-12 day.
ETV_reference: ["Qian et al. (2009)", "Qian et al. (2010)", "Qian et al. (2013)", "Camurdan et al. (2012)", "Beuermann et al. (2012)", "Pulley et al. (2015)", "Pulley et al. (2018)", "Bogensberger et al. (2017)"]

Name: TIC 454140642
ETV_selection_reason: Clear apsidal motion detected in phase-folded photometry; dynamical interactions between the two binaries indicated.
ETV_notes: The paper reports the system as two eclipsing binaries with photometry showing clear apsidal motion, indicating dynamical interactions between the binaries.

Name: TIC 167692429
ETV_selection_reason: Third companion star inferred from ETVs exhibiting signatures of strong 3rd-body perturbations; simultaneous photodynamical modelling of TESS and WASP lightcurves and ETV curves.
ETV_notes: Eccentric triple: inner binary P1=10.26 d, e1=0.17, q1=0.99; third star P2=331.5 d, e2=0.56, imut=27 deg, q2=0.34. Orbital plane precession period ~70 yr, with ~11 yr-long eclipse intervals. One likely outer eclipsing event near end of WASP observations in 2012.

Name: TIC 220397947
ETV_selection_reason: Third companion star inferred from ETVs exhibiting signatures of strong 3rd-body perturbations; discrepancy between WASP and TESS eclipse times led to hypothesis of an additional fourth component.
ETV_notes: Inner triple system very flat, mutual inclination ~0.6 deg. Outer orbital solution ambiguous; presence of fourth component questionable.

Name: EPIC 212096658
ETV_selection_reason: Mentioned as known quadruple system whose fourth component was found through ETV residuals and systemic RV deviations.
ETV_notes: Comparison system to TIC 220397947; RV observations covered more than 4.5 outermost orbital cycles, so presence of fourth star seems certain.

Name: UZ For
ETV_selection_reason: Paper performs O-C analysis and fits a two-planet LTTE model to eclipse timing variations.
ETV_notes: Two circumbinary planets proposed: first elliptical term P3=14.67(1) yr, e3=0.69(1), M3,min=10.00(2) M_Jup; second P4=5.82(3) yr, e4=0.45(6), M4,min=3.22(5) M_Jup. Significant residuals remain; possible cyclic magnetic activity may contribute a quasi-periodic term. Quadratic term A=-14.5(2)x10^-14. Combined binary mass assumed 0.84 Msol.

Name: Kepler-451
ETV_selection_reason: Paper performs ETV analysis on the eclipsing binary Kepler-451, including frequency analysis of O-C residuals and modeling with two LiTEs and a secular change.
ETV_notes: The paper uses primary eclipse timings from Kepler and TESS. A 3.7-day periodicity with amplitude ~2.8 s in the Kepler ETV diagram is identified as spurious (caused by sampling and sdB pulsations) and ignored. For this spurious signal, assuming LiTE would imply a minimum mass of ~0.044 Msol and minimum semi-major axis of 0.038 au, but it is rejected. The long-term variations are modeled with two LiTEs (interpreted as circumbinary planets) plus a secular period decrease due to magnetic stellar winds. The paper does not report final model parameters or conclusions in the extracted text.

Name: RR Cae
ETV_selection_reason: ETV analysis of RR Cae with cyclic O-C variations fitted by LTTE models for one or two circumbinary objects.
ETV_notes: The one-object LTTE model gives a cyclic variation of 16.6±0.2 yr with amplitude 14±1 s and minimum mass 3.4±0.2 MJup (reduced chi-square 8.55). The preferred two-object model gives amplitudes 12±1 s and 20±5 s with periods 15.0±0.5 yr and 39±5 yr, corresponding to M3 sin i3 = 3.0±0.3 MJup and M4 sin i4 = 2.7±0.7 MJup (reduced chi-square 4.82). Known planet RR Cae b has 4.2 MJup and period 11.9 yr (Qian et al. 2012). Applegate mechanism and out-of-eclipse slope effects were tested and are not the primary driving source.

Name: RR Lyn

Optimal TESS periods range from 9.945120 to 9.945168 d, differing from the long-term period near 9.94507108 d. Name: RR Cae
ETV_selection_reason: The paper performs eclipse timing variation analysis of RR Cae, modeling the O-C diagram with one/two circumbinary-object LTT models and testing Applegate and starspot alternatives.
ETV_notes: RR Cae is a known ETV system with a circumbinary planet (RR Cae b; Qian et al. 2012). The paper analyzes O-C data from published minima and new TESS 2018/2020 minima. Qian et al. (2012) one-planet LTT model (P=11.9±0.1 yr, M sin i=4.2±0.4 MJup, a=5.3±0.6 AU at i=90 deg) does not fit the 2018-2020 minima. New MCMC fits: one-circumbinary-object model has P=16.6±0.2 yr, M sin i=3.4±0.2 MJup, a=5.55±0.05 AU (at i=90 deg), log K=-3.78, dP/dE=-1.2e-12 d/cycle, chi2=8.55. Two-circumbinary-object model has periods 15.0±0.6 yr and 39±5 yr, M sin i=3.0±0.3 MJup and 2.7±0.7 MJup, a=5.2±0.1 AU and 9.7±0.9 AU (at i=90 deg), a' sin i=0.024±0.002 AU and 0.040±0.009 AU, f(m)=6e-8 Msol and 4e-8 Msol, chi2=4.82. Authors caution it is hard to conclude two circumbinary objects because the two-object solution differs from the one-planet solution by only the Krzeminski (1984) eclipse time. The Applegate mechanism requires 18-20 times the available energy of the M dwarf and cannot drive the variation; out-of-eclipse slope contributes <1e-5 d and is not the primary source. REBOUND simulations show both one- and two-object configurations are stable over 1.7 Myr.

Name: BU CMi
ETV_selection_reason: ETV analysis via photodynamical modelling; eclipse timing variations, outer-orbit period, and apsidal motion investigated.
ETV_notes: BU CMi is a 2+2 quadruple system consisting of two short-period eclipsing binaries (A and B), claimed to be the tightest known quadruple with P_out ~121.5 d. Photodynamical modelling of TESS photometry, eclipse timings, and RVs explains the ETV changes with the 121-day outer orbit, establishes longer-term ETV variability on a ~1200-day period, and predicts rapid apsidal motions in the EBs on ~25-year timescales. Volkov et al. (2021) found P=6.62 yr and attributed the 121-day ETV variations to a 'nutation' effect; the present work rules this out. The best-fit model in Fig. 8 uses P_out=121.75 d.

This paper adds 18 new primary minima (2019 Jun - 2022 Feb) and finds a quadratic ephemeris provides a marginally better fit: BJD_min=2445730.5567(3)+0.116719542(6)E-1.85(36)e-13 E^2.

Name: NY Vir (PG1336-018)

Name: QS Vir

ETV_notes: The paper revisits QS Vir ETVs. Previous studies proposed diverse interpretations: Qian et al. (2010) suggested a circumbinary planet (~7 MJup) plus continuous orbital period reduction; Parsons et al. (2010) favored a broader eccentric orbit for a single companion; Almeida & Jablonski (2011) proposed two circumbinary objects (giant planet and brown dwarf), later shown dynamically unstable by Horner et al. (2013). This work uses 105 eclipse times covering 22.9 yr, assuming the O-C variations are due to a single companion. Best-fit companion mass 57.71 MJup (range ~40-64 MJup), eccentricity e=0.91+0.07-0.17, period P=16.69+0.47-0.42 yr. Authors state additional observations are required and caution against modeling a fourth body unless new observations modify the computed parameters.

Name: GSC 08814-01026
ETV_selection_reason: O-C analysis of eclipse timings reveals two possible periodic ETV signals; a companion is detected around the eclipsing binary.
ETV_notes: Two possible periods: 146.170 d (e2=0.98, f(m3)=1.7756 Msol, red.chi2=23.84) and 245.006 d (e2=0.32, f(m3)=0.0058 Msol, red.chi2=18.89). The 146 d LPP solution would require a ~3.6 Msol star and is likely an artefact of stellar activity/spot migration. No significant anti-correlation between primary and secondary ETV is found, but secondary ETV are sparse. Radial velocity follow-up recommended to confirm the companion.

Name: EXO 0748-676
ETV_selection_reason: The paper performs O-C diagram analysis of eclipse timings, revealing significant timing residuals and period variability.
ETV_notes: Constant-period fit to USA/RXTE data is poor (reduced chi2=84.8 for 127 dof, rms 2.94 s). A non-zero period-derivative model is also poor (reduced chi2=68.0). For all published timings, a constant Pdot model gives reduced chi2=121.1 for 170 dof; a two-period model gives reduced chi2=67.3 for 169 dof with period change Porb,1-Porb,0 = 7.87 +/- 0.06 ms. Residuals may be interpreted as a sudden period change but likely an artifact of sparse sampling; intrinsic period jitter on timescales as short as one orbital cycle is observed.

Third-body and apsidal motion models discarded; magnetic activity cycle (Applegate mechanism) favored.

Name: V2051 Oph
ETV_selection_reason: Cyclical, quasi-periodic orbital period changes detected in O-C analysis
ETV_notes: Orbital period shows cyclical quasi-periodic changes of amplitude 17 s on a timescale of about 22 yr. No evidence of secular period increase/decrease. 3-sigma upper limit |Pdot| < 3e-12 day/day, tau_P > 5.6e7 yr. Fractional period change Delta P/P = 1.6e-7. Best explanation: solar-type magnetic activity cycle in the secondary star (Applegate mechanism). Apsidal motion and third-body explanations discarded. Mass transfer rate upper limit Mdot2 < 4.3e-9 Msol/yr (for M2=0.15 Msol).

Fractional period change Delta P/P = 4.7e-7. Best explanation: solar-type magnetic activity cycle in the secondary star (Applegate mechanism). Apsidal motion and third-body explanations discarded. Mass transfer rate upper limit Mdot2 < 1.5e-8 Msol/yr (for M2=0.09 Msol). Amplitude of cyclical modulation not quoted in text.

Name: V2051 Oph
ETV_detection_significance_description: Statistical significance of the linear plus sinusoidal ephemeris with respect to the linear fit; larger than 99.99 per cent; F(3,17)=65.6
ETV_selection_reason: O-C diagram and ephemeris fitting reveal cyclical period changes
ETV_notes: Quadratic ephemeris has statistical significance of 98.6 per cent (F(3,19)=7.2), below 3-sigma. Best-fit modulation period 22±2 yr. Linear plus sinusoidal ephemeris is not a complete description of the data (χ2ν2 > 1), indicating the period variation is not sinusoidal or not strictly periodic. Separate fits: first half of data (E<75000 cycles) described by cycle periods of 11 and 5.5 yr; second half (E>75000 cycles) best-fit period same as whole data set and also describable by 11 and 7 yr; 7 yr period consistent with 6.87 yr cycle found by Echevarria & Alvares (1993). 11, 7, and 5.5 yr are, respectively, the first, second, and third harmonics of the 22 yr main period. Large dispersion in individual timings partly attributed to flickering and to the variety of measurement methods; none of the individual literature timings correspond to the white dwarf mid-eclipse.
TimingSystematicsDescription: Large-amplitude flickering distorts the eclipse shape and affects eclipse timing measurements. The large dispersion in individual eclipse timings is partly attributed to the highly variable eclipse shape and partly to the variety of methods used by different authors; times of minimum light and of the eclipse centroid are later than the white dwarf mid-eclipse time.

Name: V4140 Sgr
ETV_detection_significance_description: Statistical significance of the linear plus sinusoidal ephemeris with respect to the linear fit; F(3,7)=49.8
ETV_selection_reason: O-C diagram and ephemeris fitting reveal cyclical period changes
ETV_notes: Fits to 12 mid-eclipse timings. Quadratic ephemeris significant at 98.3 per cent (F(3,9)=8.5), below 3-sigma; quadratic coefficient c=(+1.8±0.5)e-13 d, a factor of 2.4 smaller than derived by Baptista et al. (1992). Linear plus sinusoidal ephemeris significant at 99.97 per cent and reduces dispersion by a factor of 2 relative to the quadratic; modulation period 6.9±0.3 yr (=C=(41±2)e3 cycles); amplitude A=(19±6)e-5 d; B=(3±2)e3 cycles. Reduced chi-square: linear 4.2 (nu=10), quadratic 1.74 (nu=9), sinusoidal 0.71 (nu=7); sigma: 2.62e-3, 1.88e-3, 0.92e-3 cycles. Search for variable or harmonic cycle periods inconclusive because of the small number of timings. Timing accuracy better than 12 s. Parenthetical uncertainties in Table 6 are 1-sigma formal errors in the last quoted digits; eclipse timing errors in Table 5 parentheses are in the last digit.
TimingSystematicsDescription: UT-TDT scale difference changed by 6 s over the 16 yr span; amplitude of the difference between baricentric and heliocentric corrections is about 4 s; individual timings show a tendency to be later than the white dwarf mid-eclipse timing of the ensemble.
